claim: pCharme is a chromatin-associated lncRNA whose functional knockout in mice results in defective myogenesis and morphological remodeling of the cardiac muscle.
source: We recently identified pCharme, a chromatin-associated lncRNA whose functional knockout in mice results in defective myogenesis and morphological remodeling of the cardiac muscle.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous research findings referenced in the abstract.

claim: pCharme is specifically restricted to cardiomyocytes since the early steps of cardiomyogenesis.
source: Since the early steps of cardiomyogenesis, we found the lncRNA being specifically restricted to cardiomyocytes, where it assists the formation of specific nuclear condensates containing MATR3, as well as important RNAs for cardiac development.
evidence: This claim is supported by CAGE, scRNA sequencing, and WISH analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: pCharme assists the formation of specific nuclear condensates containing MATR3 and important RNAs for cardiac development.
source: Since the early steps of cardiomyogenesis, we found the lncRNA being specifically restricted to cardiomyocytes, where it assists the formation of specific nuclear condensates containing MATR3, as well as important RNAs for cardiac development.
evidence: This claim is supported by CLIP-seq and immunofluorescence data showing pCharme/MATR3 interaction and condensate formation.

claim: pCharme ablation in mice results in a delayed maturation of cardiomyocytes.
source: In line with the functional significance of these activities, pCharme ablation in mice results in a delayed maturation of cardiomyocytes, which ultimately leads to morphological alterations of the ventricular myocardium.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptomic analyses and phenotypic characterization of CharmeKO hearts.

claim: Delayed maturation of cardiomyocytes ultimately leads to morphological alterations of the ventricular myocardium.
source: In line with the functional significance of these activities, pCharme ablation in mice results in a delayed maturation of cardiomyocytes, which ultimately leads to morphological alterations of the ventricular myocardium.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analyses showing altered myocardium structure in CharmeKO mice.

claim: Congenital anomalies in myocardium are clinically relevant in humans and predispose patients to major complications.
source: Since congenital anomalies in myocardium are clinically relevant in humans and predispose patients to major complications, the identification of novel genes controlling cardiac morphology becomes crucial.
evidence: This claim draws from established medical knowledge about congenital heart defects.

claim: Heart development occurs through a cascade of events in which a subtle equilibrium between proliferation, migration, and differentiation ultimately leads precursor cells to mature into all the major cardiac cell types.
source: In all vertebrates, heart development occurs through a cascade of events in which a subtle equilibrium between proliferation, migration, and differentiation ultimately leads precursor cells to mature into all the major cardiac cell types (Bruneau, 2013; Moorman and Christoffels, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on heart development.

claim: Alteration of the developmental program results in abnormal cardiac morphogenesis and other congenital heart defects.
source: Alteration of this process results in abnormal cardiac morphogenesis and other congenital heart defects that in humans represent the most common types of birth defects and cause of infant death (Zimmerman et al., 2020; Srivastava, 2006; Center for Disease Control and Prevention, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological and clinical studies.

claim: Congenital heart defects in humans represent the most common types of birth defects and cause of infant death.
source: Alteration of this process results in abnormal cardiac morphogenesis and other congenital heart defects that in humans represent the most common types of birth defects and cause of infant death (Zimmerman et al., 2020; Srivastava, 2006; Center for Disease Control and Prevention, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological data.

claim: Only 15–20% of all congenital heart defects have been associated to known genetic conditions.
source: Mutations of transcription factors and their protein cofactors have emerged as causative of a broad spectrum of heart malformations, although only 15–20% of all congenital heart defects have been associated to known genetic conditions (Morton et al., 2022; Kodo et al., 2009; Bouveret et al., 2015; Ang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to genetic studies of congenital heart defects.

claim: LncRNAs form a heterogeneous class of non-protein coding transcripts, longer than 200 nucleotides.
source: LncRNAs form a heterogeneous class of non-protein coding transcripts, longer than 200 nucleotides, participating in many physiological (i.e., cell stemness, differentiation, or tissue development) and pathological (i.e., cancer, inflammation, cardiovascular, or neurodegeneration) processes (Mirzadeh Azad et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2018; Riva et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature defining lncRNAs.

claim: LncRNAs participate in many physiological and pathological processes.
source: LncRNAs form a heterogeneous class of non-protein coding transcripts, longer than 200 nucleotides, participating in many physiological (i.e., cell stemness, differentiation, or tissue development) and pathological (i.e., cancer, inflammation, cardiovascular, or neurodegeneration) processes (Mirzadeh Azad et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2018; Riva et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on lncRNA functions.

claim: Charme is a mammalian conserved lncRNA gene whose loss of function in mice causes progressive myopathy and congenital heart remodeling.
source: Along this line, in 2015 we identified a new collection of muscle-specific lncRNAs (Ballarino et al., 2015) and focused our attention on Charme (Chromatin architect of muscle expression) (mm9 chr7:51,728,798–51,740,770), a mammalian conserved lncRNA gene, whose loss of function in mice causes progressive myopathy and, intriguingly, congenital heart remodeling (Ballarino et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The Charme locus shows highest expression during development (E11-E15) followed by a gradual decrease at postnatal stages.
source: In addition to its cardiac specificity, this profiling revealed the highest expression of the locus during development (E11-E15) followed by a gradual decrease at postnatal stages (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by FANTOM5 CAGE-seq data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Both pCharme and mCharme isoforms are more expressed at the fetal than the postnatal stage.
source: RT-qPCR analyses with specific primers confirmed the CAGE output and revealed that both the isoforms are more expressed at the fetal than the postnatal stage (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: pCharme is 50% more abundant than mCharme at fetal stages.
source: More importantly, we found pCharme to be 50% more abundant than mCharme, which is particularly intriguing in consideration of the prominent role of the nuclear isoform previously shown in skeletal myogenesis (Desideri et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data and citation to previous work.

claim: Charme locus expression is initially detected in the tubular heart at E8.5.
source: These analyses revealed an initial expression of Charme locus already in the tubular heart (Figure 1C, E8.5), within territories which will give rise to the future atria and ventricles (V), with the inflow (IFT) and outflow (OFT) tracts displaying the highest signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The inflow and outflow tracts display the highest Charme signals at E8.5.
source: These analyses revealed an initial expression of Charme locus already in the tubular heart (Figure 1C, E8.5), within territories which will give rise to the future atria and ventricles (V), with the inflow (IFT) and outflow (OFT) tracts displaying the highest signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: pCharme expression is restricted to cardiomyocytes in embryonal hearts at E12.5.
source: Upon clustering (Figure 1E, upper panel) the different cardiac cell types based on the expression of representative marker genes (Li et al., 2016; Jackson-Weaver et al., 2020; Franco et al., 2006; Meilhac and Buckingham, 2018; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E), we found pCharme expression restricted to cardiomyocytes, with an almost identical distribution between the atrial (CM-A), ventricular (CM-V), and other (CM-VP, CM-IVS, CM-OFT) cell clusters (Figure 1E, lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: pCharme shows an almost identical distribution between atrial, ventricular, and other cardiomyocyte clusters.
source: Upon clustering (Figure 1E, upper panel) the different cardiac cell types based on the expression of representative marker genes (Li et al., 2016; Jackson-Weaver et al., 2020; Franco et al., 2006; Meilhac and Buckingham, 2018; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E), we found pCharme expression restricted to cardiomyocytes, with an almost identical distribution between the atrial (CM-A), ventricular (CM-V), and other (CM-VP, CM-IVS, CM-OFT) cell clusters (Figure 1E, lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TBX5 transcription factor has canonical motifs and enriched sites in the pCharme promoter.
source: Searching for cardiac regulators, we identified canonical motifs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) and enriched sites (Figure 1F) for the T-box transcription factor-5 (TBX5).
evidence: This claim is supported by in silico analysis of the pCharme promoter.

claim: TBX5 is a key regulator of heart development known to activate genes associated to CM maturation in early development and morphogenesis at later stages.
source: In addition to being a key regulator of heart development, known to activate genes associated to CM maturation in early development and morphogenesis at later stages (Nadadur et al., 2016; Steimle and Moskowitz, 2017), TBX5 was recently found to control the expression of several lncRNAs (Yang et al., 2017), a subset of them intriguingly enriched, as for pCharme, in the chromatin fraction of cardiomyocytes (Hall et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on TBX5 function.

claim: TBX5 was recently found to control the expression of several lncRNAs.
source: In addition to being a key regulator of heart development, known to activate genes associated to CM maturation in early development and morphogenesis at later stages (Nadadur et al., 2016; Steimle and Moskowitz, 2017), TBX5 was recently found to control the expression of several lncRNAs (Yang et al., 2017), a subset of them intriguingly enriched, as for pCharme, in the chromatin fraction of cardiomyocytes (Hall et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on TBX5 and lncRNAs.

claim: pCharme positively correlates with Tbx5 in cardiomyocytes.
source: A more in-depth analysis of the scRNA-seq dataset (Jackson-Weaver et al., 2020), revealed a positive and highly significant correlation between Tbx5 and pCharme (Figure 1G, left panel) in CM, with some differences occurring across the CM cluster subtypes (see, for instance, CM-IVS/CM-OFT, Figure 1G, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq correlation analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: pCharme positively correlates with markers of cardiomyocyte identity such as Myl2 and Myl4.
source: To note, pCharme positively correlates with markers of cardiomyocyte identity, such as the Myosin light chain 2 (Myl2) and 4 (Myl4), while significant anticorrelation was found for the Kruppel-like factor 2 (Klf2) and the Twist family BHLH TF 1 (Twist1) transcripts, that respectively mark endothelial and neural crest cells (Jackson-Weaver et al., 2020; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq correlation analysis.

claim: pCharme shows significant anticorrelation with Klf2 and Twist1 transcripts that mark endothelial and neural crest cells.
source: To note, pCharme positively correlates with markers of cardiomyocyte identity, such as the Myosin light chain 2 (Myl2) and 4 (Myl4), while significant anticorrelation was found for the Kruppel-like factor 2 (Klf2) and the Twist family BHLH TF 1 (Twist1) transcripts, that respectively mark endothelial and neural crest cells (Jackson-Weaver et al., 2020; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq correlation analysis and citations.

claim: TBX5 occupies the pCharme promoter in both progenitor and differentiated cardiomyocytes, with increased occupancy during differentiation.
source: In both conditions, ChIP-seq analyses revealed the specific occupancy of TBX5 to highly conserved spots within the pCharme promoter, which increases with differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: pCharme expression is decreased by TBX5 knockout in progenitor cardiomyocytes but not in differentiated cardiomyocytes.
source: However, while in differentiated cardiomyocytes pCharme expression was insensitive to TBX5 ablation, the lncRNA abundance was consistently decreased by TBX5 knockout in progenitor cells (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: RNA-seq analysis of CharmeWT and CharmeKO neonatal hearts led to the identification of 913 differentially expressed genes.
source: RNA-seq analysis of whole hearts led to the identification of 913 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (false discovery rate [FDR] <0.1, WT vs. KO, Supplementary file 2), 573 of which were upregulated and 340 were downregulated in CharmeKO hearts (pCharme included) (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 573 genes were upregulated and 340 were downregulated in CharmeKO neonatal hearts.
source: RNA-seq analysis of whole hearts led to the identification of 913 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (false discovery rate [FDR] <0.1, WT vs. KO, Supplementary file 2), 573 of which were upregulated and 340 were downregulated in CharmeKO hearts (pCharme included) (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No differentially expressed genes were found within the neighboring chromatin environment (370 kb around Charme).
source: Similar to pCharme activity in skeletal myocytes (Ballarino et al., 2018), we did not find DEGs within the neighboring chromatin environment (370 kb around Charme) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and citation to previous work.

claim: Upregulated DEGs in CharmeKO hearts are primarily enriched in cell cycle and cell division categories.
source: These analyses revealed that the upregulated DEGs were primarily enriched (FDR-values < 1,0E-10) in cell cycle and cell division categories (Figure 2D, left panel), which parallels with a slight increase in the number of KI-67+ mitotic CharmeKO nuclei, as quantified from neonatal cardiac sections (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D and KI-67 staining data.

claim: CharmeKO neonatal hearts show a slight increase in the number of KI-67+ mitotic nuclei.
source: These analyses revealed that the upregulated DEGs were primarily enriched (FDR-values < 1,0E-10) in cell cycle and cell division categories (Figure 2D, left panel), which parallels with a slight increase in the number of KI-67+ mitotic CharmeKO nuclei, as quantified from neonatal cardiac sections (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by KI-67 immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Downregulated DEGs in CharmeKO hearts are enriched in anatomical structure morphogenesis and circulatory system development categories.
source: The same study was applied to the downregulated DEGs, which revealed their enrichment to more functional and morphogenetic GO categories and primarily referred to anatomical structure morphogenesis (FDR 5.77E-07) and circulatory system development (FDR 3.1338E-06) (Figure 2D, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The expression of genes in the anatomical structure morphogenesis category is significantly decreased in CharmeKO hearts from E15.5 onward.
source: By expanding the analysis from neonatal to embryonal timepoints (E12.5, E15.5, and E18.5), we found that the expression of these genes was significantly decreased upon pCharme ablation from the fetal E15.5 stage onward,as compared to WT (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The Myh6/Myh7 ratio displays a gradual decrease in CharmeKO hearts from E15.5 onward.
source: Similarly, the Myh6/Myh7 ratio, which measures CM maturation (England and Loughna, 2013; Scheuermann and Boyer, 2013) and that increases over the wild-type timepoints, displays a gradual decrease in the CharmeKO hearts from E15.5 onward (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2F and citations.

claim: The Myh6/Myh7 ratio measures cardiomyocyte maturation.
source: Similarly, the Myh6/Myh7 ratio, which measures CM maturation (England and Loughna, 2013; Scheuermann and Boyer, 2013) and that increases over the wild-type timepoints, displays a gradual decrease in the CharmeKO hearts from E15.5 onward (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on cardiomyocyte maturation markers.

claim: The expression of cell-cycle and proliferation genes was not affected by pCharme ablation during embryonal development (E12.5, E15.5, E18.5).
source: To note, the expression of cell-cycle and proliferation genes was not affected by pCharme ablation over the same developmental window (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The upregulation of cell-cycle genes in neonatal CharmeKO hearts is likely a consequence of cardiac maturation impairment.
source: Hence, we argue that their upregulation in neonatal KO hearts was likely a consequence of the cardiac maturation impairment, which leads to a shift to a more fetal and proliferative state of cardiomyocytes upon birth.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the developmental expression patterns observed.

claim: CharmeKO hearts at E15.5 show a pronounced alteration of the myocardium with a clear decrease of the area of the ventricular cavities.
source: Accordingly, histological analyses performed by hematoxylin and eosin staining of CharmeWT and CharmeKO cardiac cryo-sections (E15.5) showed a pronounced alteration of the myocardium, with a clear decrease of the area of the ventricular cavities (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: CharmeKO hearts display a significant reduction of NPPA+ tissues at E15.5.
source: We found that, with respect to WT, mutant hearts display a significant reduction of NPPA+ tissues (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), which parallels the decreased expression of the Irx3 and Sema3a trabecular markers (Choquet et al., 2019; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), and the diminished density of the capillary endothelium imaged by lectin staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: CharmeKO hearts show decreased expression of the Irx3 and Sema3a trabecular markers.
source: We found that, with respect to WT, mutant hearts display a significant reduction of NPPA+ tissues (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), which parallels the decreased expression of the Irx3 and Sema3a trabecular markers (Choquet et al., 2019; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), and the diminished density of the capillary endothelium imaged by lectin staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and citation.

claim: CharmeKO hearts show diminished density of the capillary endothelium.
source: We found that, with respect to WT, mutant hearts display a significant reduction of NPPA+ tissues (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), which parallels the decreased expression of the Irx3 and Sema3a trabecular markers (Choquet et al., 2019; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), and the diminished density of the capillary endothelium imaged by lectin staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by lectin staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: CharmeKO mice show progressive deterioration of systolic function that becomes significant at 9 months of age.
source: Overall, these ensure the preservation of the cardiac function and structure in adulthood, as a progressive deterioration of the systolic function, which becomes significant at 9 months of age (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I; Supplementary file 3), was observed in CharmeKO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by echocardiography data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I.

claim: pCharme mainly localizes in the nucleus while mCharme is enriched in the cytoplasm in fetal cardiomyocytes.
source: RT-qPCR analyses revealed that, in line with what was previously observed in skeletal muscle, in cardiomyocytes pCharme mainly localizes in the nucleus, while the fully spliced mCharme is enriched in the cytoplasm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by subcellular fractionation and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: pCharme exhibits a punctuate nuclear localization pattern in fetal cardiomyocytes.
source: In agreement with the subcellular fractionation, the imaging experiments confirmed the nuclear localization of pCharme, which exhibits its typical punctuate pattern.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: pCharme and MATR3 colocalize in the nucleus of fetal cardiomyocytes and form nuclear condensates.
source: Further analysis of the three-dimensional distribution of pCharme and MATR3 revealed a clear colocalization of their signals and the formation of nuclear condensates, as quantified by 3D Pearson's correlation coefficient applied to the overlapping signals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by IF/RNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3B and quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MATR3-positive condensates appear more diffuse in CharmeKO cardiac muscles compared to wild-type.
source: Coherently with their pCharme-dependent formation, these condensates appeared more diffuse in tissues where the lncRNA is not expressed, as CharmeKO muscles and WT spinal cords (Figure 3C, middle and lower panels; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by MATR3 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MATR3 immunofluorescence pattern is less discrete and more homogeneous in CharmeKO cardiomyocyte nuclei compared to wild-type.
source: More accurate quantification of the MATR3 fluorescence distribution in the nucleus of CharmeKO cardiomyocytes (coefficient of variation [CV], Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) revealed a MATR3 IF pattern that was less discrete and more homogeneous in respect to WT.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of MATR3 fluorescence distribution shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: MATR3 CLIP-seq from fetal hearts identified 952 cardiac-expressed transcripts significantly bound by MATR3 in wild-type hearts.
source: Subsequent analysis of the RNA led to the identification of 952 cardiac-expressed transcripts significantly bound by MATR3 in the WT heart (log2 fold enrichment >2 and FDR value <0.05, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by MATR3 CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Most of MATR3 enrichment is located within the introns of protein-coding mRNA precursors.
source: In line with the binding propensities exhibited by MATR3 in other cell systems (Uemura et al., 2017), most of its enrichment was located within the introns of protein-coding mRNA precursors (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by MATR3 CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B and citation.

claim: pCharme is at the top of the MATR3 interactors in CharmeWT fetal hearts.
source: Strikingly, even though the class of lncRNAs was poorly represented (Figure 4B, upper panel), we found pCharme at the top of the MATR3 interactors in CharmeWT hearts (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by MATR3 CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 4.

claim: MATR3 specifically binds to pCharme but not mCharme in wild-type fetal hearts.
source: Further quantification of the retrieved RNAs by RT-qPCR evidenced the specific enrichment of pCharme, but not mCharme, in the wild-type samples, which supports the distinctive binding of MATR3 to the nuclear isoform (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR validation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There is a strong reduction of MATR3-CLIP signal across Charme RNA in CharmeKO samples.
source: As expected, we observed a strong reduction of MATR3-CLIP signal across Charme RNA in CharmeKO samples (Figure 4C; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by MATR3 CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The MATR3 consensus sequence (UUCUU) is among the most over-represented pyrimidine-enriched motifs in MATR3 CLIP peaks.
source: Enrichment analysis performed by using 93 RNA-binding motifs catalogued by the CISBP-RNA database (Ray et al., 2013) pinpointed the MATR3 consensus sequence (UUCUU, Desideri et al., 2020) among the most over-represented pyrimidine-enriched motifs (E value < 0.05) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4D and citations.

claim: The MATR3 motif is positioned at the peak summit close to the strongest enrichment of MATR3.
source: When analyzed in respect to the intensity of the CLIP signals, the MATR3 motif was positioned at the peak summit (±50 nt) (Figure 4E), close to the strongest enrichment of MATR3, thus suggesting a direct and highly specific binding of the protein to these sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by positional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: 'Heart development' is the most significantly enriched functional category for protein-coding transcripts directly bound by MATR3 in wild-type fetal hearts.
source: Encouraged by this quality assessment, we finally performed a GO enrichment analysis on the 881 protein-coding transcripts directly bound by MATR3 in the WT heart and found 'heart development' as the most significantly enriched functional category (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The expression of MATR3-bound RNAs is globally reduced by pCharme knockout in the heart.
source: On a transcriptome scale, we found that in the heart the expression of MATR3-bound RNAs was globally reduced by pCharme knockout (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 12% of the downregulated DEGs (41 out of 340) in CharmeKO hearts are bound by MATR3.
source: Indeed, while MATR3 targets were under-represented among transcripts whose expression was unaffected (invariant) or increased (upregulated) by pCharme ablation, 12% of the downregulated DEGs (41 out of 340, pCharme included) were bound by MATR3 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by integration of RNA-seq and CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Common MATR3/pCharme targets are significantly enriched across the top three GO classes for CharmeKO downregulated genes.
source: To note, these common targets were significantly enriched across the top three GO classes, previously defined for CharmeKO downregulated genes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The main consequence of pCharme depletion is a significant decrease of MATR3 enrichment on RNA.
source: Among the shared peaks, DB revealed that the main consequence of pCharme depletion was a significant decrease of MATR3 enrichment on the RNA (Figure 5C, Loss), while the increase of protein binding was observed on a lower fraction of peaks (Figure 5C, Gain).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential binding analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Loss peaks are significantly enriched in a subset (20 out of 40, 50%) of downregulated DEGs.
source: By mapping these differentially bound regions to the MATR3 targets that are also responsive to pCharme ablation (DEGs), we found that while the gained peaks were equally distributed, the loss peaks were significantly enriched in a subset (20 out of 40, 50%) of downregulated DEGs (Figure 5D, upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential binding analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The majority (13 out of 20) of downregulated DEGs with loss peaks play important roles in embryo development, anatomical structure morphogenesis, and development of the circulatory system.
source: Overall, these results suggest that cooperation between pCharme and MATR3 activities is needed for the expression of specific RNAs, where the majority (13 out of 20) is known to play important roles in embryo development, anatomical structure morphogenesis, and development of the circulatory system (Figure 5D, lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential binding analysis and GO annotation shown in Figure 5D.

claim: MATR3 depletion in primary cardiac cells leads to downregulation of Cacna1c, Notch3, and Myo18b.
source: RT-qPCR analysis revealed that three out of four tested genes exhibited a significant expression decrease upon MATR3 depletion (Figure 5E, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from MATR3 knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: pCharme was previously found to play an epigenetic, architectural function in skeletal myogenesis under physiological circumstances.
source: In fact, of the two different splicing isoforms produced by the Charme locus, only the unspliced and nuclear pCharme isoform was found to play an epigenetic, architectural function in skeletal myogenesis under physiological circumstances.
evidence: This claim is based on previous research findings.

claim: The temporal and cell-type-specific expression of pCharme is critical for the activation of pro-differentiation cardiac genes during development.
source: We show that the temporal and cell-type-specific expression of pCharme is critical for the activation of pro-differentiation cardiac genes during development.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined results of expression profiling and functional studies.

claim: pCharme activity relies on the formation of pCharme-dependent RNA-rich condensates acting as chromatin hubs for MATR3.
source: Mechanistically, we provide evidence that this activity relies on the formation of pCharme-dependent RNA-rich condensates acting as chromatin hubs for MATR3, a nuclear matrix DNA/RNA-binding protein highly abundant in the fetal heart and source, upon mutation, of congenital defects (Quintero-Rivera et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by CLIP-seq and imaging data showing pCharme/MATR3 interaction and condensate formation, along with citation.

claim: MATR3 is a nuclear matrix DNA/RNA-binding protein highly abundant in the fetal heart.
source: Mechanistically, we provide evidence that this activity relies on the formation of pCharme-dependent RNA-rich condensates acting as chromatin hubs for MATR3, a nuclear matrix DNA/RNA-binding protein highly abundant in the fetal heart and source, upon mutation, of congenital defects (Quintero-Rivera et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on MATR3.

claim: Mutations in MATR3 are a source of congenital defects.
source: Mechanistically, we provide evidence that this activity relies on the formation of pCharme-dependent RNA-rich condensates acting as chromatin hubs for MATR3, a nuclear matrix DNA/RNA-binding protein highly abundant in the fetal heart and source, upon mutation, of congenital defects (Quintero-Rivera et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on MATR3 mutations.

claim: In the absence of pCharme, the nuclear distribution of MATR3 is altered in developing cardiomyocytes.
source: We show that, in the absence of the lncRNA, the nuclear distribution of MATR3 was altered in developing cardiomyocytes as well as its binding to specific RNAs, with a consequent mis-regulation of their expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing altered MATR3 distribution in CharmeKO hearts.

claim: In the absence of pCharme, MATR3 binding to specific RNAs is altered, with a consequent mis-regulation of their expression.
source: We show that, in the absence of the lncRNA, the nuclear distribution of MATR3 was altered in developing cardiomyocytes as well as its binding to specific RNAs, with a consequent mis-regulation of their expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential MATR3 CLIP-seq analysis and RNA-seq data.

claim: Adult CharmeKO mice develop a significant reduction of systolic function with initial signs of cardiac dilation.
source: In our case, adult CharmeKO mice develop a significant reduction of systolic function with initial signs of cardiac dilation, which denotes an early phase of cardiomyopathy.
evidence: This claim is supported by echocardiography data.

claim: The transition of cardiomyocytes toward an immature phenotype in vivo is associated with the development of dilated cardiomyopathy.
source: The results are supported by recently published data suggesting that the transition of cardiomyocytes toward an immature phenotype in vivo is associated with the development of dilated cardiomyopathy (Ikeda et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on cardiomyocyte maturation and cardiomyopathy.
